transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Regulus CISO), Hannah Brookes (Infra Lead), Liam O'Neill (Cloud Eng)

Summary: quick architecture walkthrough for private/VPC deployment. Focus: egress controls, KMS/HSM key custody, audit trail for SOC 2 readiness, SSO/RBAC mapping, and operational runbooks for break-glass. Customer wants minimal open egress and proof that private control plane telemetry doesn't leak data.

Topics: network zoning, bastion/egress proxy, egress allowlists, firewall/NAT behavior, KMS integration (customer-managed keys), audit logs retention and SIEM forward, SOC2 evidence paths, RBAC/SSO mapping, disaster recovery for key rotation.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, i'll kick off real quick. samir, do you want to confirm goals for today?
[00:12] Samir (Regulus CISO): yeah thanks maya. main goals, we want to understand how redwood's private control plane behaves in a VPC, what egress is required, how keys are handled — we prefer customer-managed K M S if possible — and what audit logs we can ship to our splunk cluster or security lake. and obviously SOC2 artifacts, timeline, that sort of thing.
[00:32] Maya: perfect. ethan from our infra team will run through the network flows and kms options.
[00:36] Ethan (Redwood SE): hi all, i'll start with a very high-level diagram, apologies if some terms come out a bit rough — transcriber likes to mangle things — but i'll be clear. imagine two planes: the private control plane (customer VPC) and the serving plane (could be dedicated or hosted depending on contract). in your case you want the control plane inside your VPC, so no public control-plane egress except the minimal telemetry and license check if enabled.
[01:05] Hannah (Regulus): quick question — when you say telemetry, are we talking about model payloads or just meta metrics? we cannot allow Pii leaving the VPC.
[01:12] Ethan: great question. telemetry is metadata only by default — routing latencies, instance health, token counts — but not full user prompts. we treat any model payload redaction as configurable; you can opt into zero-telemetry which basically suppresses even metadata. for SOC2 you'd typically keep metadata but we can sign a data handling addendum.
[01:33] Liam (Cloud Eng): how do you handle callback webhooks? our app needs synchronous callbacks for post-processing and those often hit vendor endpoints.
[01:39] Maya: callbacks are optional. for private you can either route callbacks through your egress proxy/bastion or use a VPC endpoint that talks to an internal queue. many customers prefer to terminate callbacks inside the VPC then push to internal services—no public outbound needed.
[01:55] Samir: okay, so minimal egress. can we get firm list of IPs/ports we need to open if we choose to allow any?
[02:02] Ethan: yes — we'll provide an allowlist. typical pattern is: allow outbound to our control plane management endpoint (TLS 443) — but in private installs that endpoint can be private peered; alternatively, we support a totally air-gapped mode where you run both control and serving and only we provide software images. for K M S, if you're bringing your own keys via cloud KMS (GCP KMS, AWS KMS, Azure KeyVault) you'll need outbound to the KMS endpoints in those cases. we'll enumerate exact FQDNs and ranges in the doc.
[02:30] Hannah: any chance of using an HSM on prem? regulatory requires FIPS 140-2 sometimes.
[02:35] Ethan: yes we integrate with customer H S M through KMIP or cloud provider HSMs. the private agent can be configured to call your HSM over a private link. note: that path requires appropriate certs and a mutual TLS (mTLS) handshake — we'll include the cert rotation recommendations.
[02:52] Speaker 2 (transcriber mislabel, likely Maya): what's the architecture for egress proxying — do you require a bastion host?
[02:58] Liam: this is key for us. we run egress through a NAT gateway now, but we'd prefer tighter policing, like an egress proxy that can do allowlist and inspect TLS SNI.
[03:07] Ethan: recommended pattern: egress proxy (Envoy/squid/nginx) in a private subnet, combined with an egress firewall that only allows TLS to specific FQDNs. for maximum control we also support a TLS termination at the proxy with re-encryption to the KMS endpoint if you need deep packet inspection — though that introduces key handling considerations.
[03:26] Samir: deep packet inspection on M L payloads is not acceptable for us — can't have LLM prompts routed through DPI.
[03:31] Ethan: understood. you can keep TLS end-to-end, we only need SNI-level allowlisting. all sensitive payloads remain encrypted to the model serving node and are not transmitted in telemetry.
[03:41] Hannah: what about audit logs — we need raw logs forwarded to our SIEM and 2 year retention for SOC2.
[03:48] Maya: we can stream audit logs (auth events, API ops, admin actions) to your syslog/splunk/secure storage via a push or a pull using a forwarder living in your VPC. retention is customer side; we can store for a short window for troubleshooting but primary archival should be your SIEM.
[04:05] Ethan: and logs include request IDs, user IDs (if passed), model version, node ID, and action type. we can optionally hash or redact user prompts before sending if you want to keep evidence of access without PII.
[04:18] Samir: hashing is interesting — we need deterministic hashes so we can link events during audits. is that available?
[04:23] Ethan: yes deterministic hashing with a salt you own — we can compute HMACs client-side in the agent before logs leave the VPC. that'll satisfy linkability without exposing raw text.
[04:35] Liam: how does key rotation work with ongoing sessions? do in-flight requests fail when keys rotate?
[04:41] Ethan: we support lazy rotation with dual-key mode: agent keeps previous key for a configurable TTL to finish in-flight sessions then flips to the new key for new sessions. this prevents abrupt failures. we'll provide sample config for rotation windows.
[04:55] Hannah: and who holds master key? we want customer master key in AWS KMS with key policy restricted to our security team.
[05:02] Maya: perfect — customer-managed CMK in KMS is supported. Redwood agents will request ephemeral data keys via KMS encrypt/decrypt calls; we never persist CMKs. we can also add an HSM-backed wrap if you want.
[05:14] Samir: for SOC2 evidence, can you provide a matrix of controls you map to our SOC2 requirements?
[05:20] Maya: yes, we've got a SOC2 evidence pack we can share — it'll map product features to common control objectives like access logging, key management, incident response, and change control. i'll attach it after the call.
[05:29] Samir: great. also curious about RBAC and SSO. our identity is okta and we require SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO.
[05:37] Ethan: we support SAML SSO and SCIM; role mappings can be enforced at the agent level for private installs. for strict separation we recommend mapping Okta groups to RBAC roles, and single admin accounts for key rotation. we can demonstrate with a sample SCIM mapping.
[05:53] Hannah: are there built-in break-glass flows? e.g., emergency bypass for a runaway job without exposing keys.
[05:59] Ethan: yes. break-glass uses a short-lived service token that is minted via a manual multi-signer process — think two-person approval in your vault. it escalates with auditing — every break-glass use is logged and forwarded to your SIEM.
[06:12] Speaker 3 (Samir): that's good. one more — what about network segmentation between model serving and internal data stores? we can't have models reach our DBs directly.
[06:20] Ethan: model serving nodes live in separate subnets and only have access to allowed internal endpoints via explicit firewall rules. no database access is required for most inference flows — you pass references or prefetch vectors within your internal network. we advise using private endpoints for any datastore calls.
[06:36] Maya: we also provide per-route network policies so you can restrict which models or routes may contact certain services.
[06:42] Liam: that sounds promising. can we talk about latency impact if we route everything through an egress proxy and KMS?
[06:50] Ethan: small overhead. KMS calls add a few tens to low hundreds of milliseconds per key fetch depending on region; that's why we recommend caching ephemeral data keys in the agent for the request window. egress proxy adds a few ms if it's in the same AZ. we'll include benchmark numbers; that's one of the things Ethan will run post-call.
[07:09] Samir: curious about disaster recovery — if your agent has a bug and cannot decrypt tokens we need an offline process to recover.
[07:16] Ethan: we provide an offline key unwrap tool and a documented recovery procedure that uses your KMS console to rewrap keys and validate agent binary. part of the SOC2 evidence will include this runbook.
[07:27] Hannah: are there known gotchas for private deployments in hybrid clouds?
[07:32] Ethan: cross-cloud networking can introduce complex routing and DNS issues. things to watch: asymmetric routing, MTU differences, and private DNS suffixes. recommend a dedicated VPC peering or transit gateway and explicit host routes.
[07:47] Samir: okay, can we get a short list of explicit firewall rules we should create to run a pilot?
[07:53] Maya: yes we'll share a pilot-ready firewall template: IPs, FQDNs, ports, and egress proxies.
[07:59] Liam: about audit trails — do you provide immutable logs or can we push to an append-only object store?
[08:05] Ethan: we can push to an append-only bucket (S3 with Object Lock) or directly to your SIEM; logs are signed and include a monotonically increasing sequence number for tamper detection.
[08:17] Samir: excellent. any regulatory data residency concerns? we operate EU and US tenants and need control plane on EU for EU customers.
[08:24] Maya: location pinning is supported — you can pin control plane and serving nodes to a region. for hybrid needs you can deploy separate private control planes per region.
[08:33] Hannah: will this increase operational overhead?
[08:36] Maya: some, but we offer automation templates (terraform modules) to standardize templates across regions.
[08:42] Ethan: quick note on licensing and updates — private control plane patches must be applied via your internal CI/CD pipeline; we recommend a canary rolling update strategy we document in the runbook.
[08:52] Samir: cool. let's recap next steps.
[08:56] Maya: recap: we will share the private deployment diagram and firewall template, ethan will run the egress/kms benchmark and share logs, and reglus will provide firewall and identity contacts. schedule: docs 2-3 days, benchmarks 1 week.
[09:12] Samir: spelled out, that's fine. any blockers?
[09:16] Maya: none on our side.
[09:18] Hannah: none. thanks everyone.
[09:22] Maya: cool, i'll send notes and the SOC2 pack. thanks all.

End of transcript.
